prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Japanese Prime Minister Taro Aso met with President Barack Obama on Tuesday making him the first head of state to be hosted by the new administration. Japanese Prime Minister Taro Aso steps off his Boeing 747 at Andrews Air Force Base in Maryland Monday. It was a long trip -- 6,800 miles (11,000 km) -- for a short meeting -- one hour -- and happened as Obama was preparing his first address to a joint session of Congress. Sitting next to Aso in the White House, Obama said: "The friendship between the United States and Japan is extraordinarily important. "It is for that reason that the prime minister is the first foreign dignitary to visit me in the Oval Office." Obama said the U.S.-Japanese alliance would be crucial in solving international problems including climate change. "We think we have to work together, not only on issues relating to the Pacific Rim, but throughout the world," Obama added. Aso said the global economy was also on the agenda at their meeting. "We are the number 1 and second biggest economies of the world. We will have to work hand in hand. "I think we are the only two nations which are powerful enough to solve those very critical, vital issue," Aso said. Japan's Cabinet Secretary Takeo Kawamura said that being the first to visit the Obama White House was an indication of the priority the new president placed on the relationship. Another topic likely to have been on the agenda was Japan's Asian neighbor North Korea, which U.S. intelligence says is preparing to test a long-range missile. Pyongyang has denied the charge, instead saying it is making preparations to launch a satellite. A test-fire by North Korea in 2006 failed 40 seconds after launch. The missile is thought to have an intended range of about 4,200 miles (6,700 kilometers), which -- if true -- could give it the capability of striking Alaska or Hawaii. Aso's visit to Washington comes, as his approval rating stands at a meager 11 percent, the second lowest ever recorded for a Japanese prime minister. Yoshiro Mori, a former prime minister, resigned after his rate bottomed out at 9 percent. Last week his finance minister Shoichi Nakagawa announced he will step down after coming under fire for appearing intoxicated at a weekend news conference during the G-7 meeting in Rome. CNN's Chie Kobayashi contributed to this report.

WASHINGTON (CNN) — Japanese Prime Minister Taro Aso met with President Barack Obama on Tuesday, becoming the first head of state to be hosted by the new administration.

Aso arrived Monday at Andrews Air Force Base in Maryland aboard his Boeing 747. It was a long journey — 6,800 miles (11,000 kilometers) — for a brief meeting of just one hour, taking place as Obama prepared to deliver his first address to a joint session of Congress.

Seated beside Aso at the White House, Obama said, “The friendship between the United States and Japan is extraordinarily important. It is for that reason that the prime minister is the first foreign dignitary to visit me in the Oval Office.”

Obama said the U.S.-Japanese alliance would be crucial in addressing international challenges, including climate change.

“We think we have to work together, not only on issues relating to the Pacific Rim, but throughout the world,” Obama added.

Aso said the global economy was also on the agenda during their meeting.

“We are the number 1 and second biggest economies of the world. We will have to work hand in hand,” Aso said. “I think we are the only two nations which are powerful enough to solve those very critical, vital issue.”

Japan’s Cabinet Secretary Takeo Kawamura said Aso’s distinction as the first leader to visit the Obama White House reflected the priority the new president placed on the U.S.-Japan relationship.

Another topic likely to have been discussed was Japan’s Asian neighbor, North Korea, which U.S. intelligence says is preparing to test a long-range missile. Pyongyang has denied the allegation, saying instead that it is preparing to launch a satellite.

A North Korean test-fire in 2006 failed 40 seconds after launch. The missile is believed to have an intended range of about 4,200 miles (6,700 kilometers), which — if accurate — could give it the capability to strike Alaska or Hawaii.

Aso’s visit to Washington comes as his approval rating stands at a meager 11 percent, the second lowest ever recorded for a Japanese prime minister. Yoshiro Mori, a former prime minister, resigned after his approval rating fell to 9 percent.

Last week, Aso’s finance minister, Shoichi Nakagawa, announced he would step down after coming under fire for appearing intoxicated at a weekend news conference during the G-7 meeting in Rome.

CNN’s Chie Kobayashi contributed to this report.

WASHINGTON (CNN) — Japanese Prime Minister Taro Aso held talks with President Barack Obama on Tuesday, becoming the first foreign leader received by the new administration.

Aso arrived Monday at Andrews Air Force Base in Maryland aboard his Boeing 747. He had traveled about 6,800 miles, or 11,000 kilometers, for a meeting scheduled to last just one hour. The visit also came as Obama was getting ready to deliver his first address to a joint session of Congress.

Seated beside Aso at the White House, Obama emphasized the importance of the countries’ ties, saying the friendship between Japan and the United States was “extraordinarily important.” He added that this was why Aso was the first foreign dignitary invited to meet with him in the Oval Office.

Obama said the U.S.-Japan alliance would play a key role in addressing global challenges, including climate change. He noted that the two nations needed to cooperate not only on matters affecting the Pacific Rim, but on issues around the world.

Aso said the worldwide economy was also part of their discussion. He pointed out that the United States and Japan were the world’s largest and second-largest economies and said they would need to work closely together. Aso added that he believed the two countries were the only nations strong enough to tackle such critical and essential problems.

Japan’s Cabinet Secretary Takeo Kawamura said Aso’s status as the first visitor to Obama’s White House showed the importance the new president attached to the bilateral relationship.

Another issue expected to have been discussed was North Korea, Japan’s neighbor in Asia. U.S. intelligence officials have said Pyongyang is preparing to test a long-range missile. North Korea has rejected that accusation, saying instead that it is getting ready to launch a satellite.

A North Korean test launch in 2006 failed 40 seconds after liftoff. The missile is believed to be designed to travel roughly 4,200 miles, or 6,700 kilometers, a range that, if accurate, could allow it to reach Alaska or Hawaii.

Aso’s trip to Washington took place while his approval rating was at just 11 percent, the second-lowest ever recorded for a Japanese prime minister. Former Prime Minister Yoshiro Mori stepped down after his approval fell to 9 percent.

The previous week, Aso’s finance minister, Shoichi Nakagawa, said he would resign after facing criticism for appearing drunk at a weekend news conference during the G-7 meeting in Rome.

CNN’s Chie Kobayashi contributed to the report.
